units.title: Being Responsible
units.intro: Grammar: must, have to and should (what you need to do), and must be / can't be / must have (guessing from a clue).

cards.title: Modals for obligation and advice
rule: **must** and **have to** = it is necessary. **must** = *I* feel it is necessary: *I **must** call my mother tonight.* **have to** = someone else made the rule (the school, the law, a doctor): *We **have to** wear a uniform at school.*
**mustn't** = it is not allowed. Don't do it! *You **mustn't** cross at a red light.* **don't have to** = it is not necessary; you can choose: *You **don't have to** bring injera; we have bread.*
**should** = it is a good idea (advice): *You **should** drink a lot of water in Massawa – it is very hot.*
After *must, should, can, might* use the **plain verb**: no *to*, no *-s*: *She must **go*** (not *must to go*, not *must goes*).
Past: use **had to** for every person: *Yesterday we **had to** walk to school because the bus broke down.*

cards.title: Must or have to? Who makes the rule?
rule: **must** and **have to** both mean *it is necessary*. The difference is **who makes the rule**.
**must** = the **speaker** feels it is necessary (my own rule or strong feeling): *I **must** study tonight – I want a good mark.* *You **must** visit us again!*
**have to / has to** = the rule comes from **outside**: a law, the school, a doctor, a timetable, a boss: *We **have to** wear a uniform at school.* *Drivers **have to** stop at a red light.*
Written rules and notices usually use **must** (the school or office is "speaking"): *Students **must** show their ID card.*
**Past:** *must* has no past form. Use **had to** for every past obligation: *Yesterday I **had to** walk to school.* **Future:** **will have to**: *You **will have to** pay next year.*
**Questions** usually use have to: *Do I have to…? Does she have to…? Did you have to…?*

cards.title: Step by step: must, have to, mustn't or don't have to?
cards.problem: Complete: (a) The doctor says I ____ take this medicine three times a day. (b) I ____ remember to buy bread – we have none left. (c) You ____ touch that wire! It is dangerous. (d) Tomorrow is a holiday, so we ____ get up early. (e) Last year my brother ____ work on Saturdays.

steps.text: **Step 1: Is it necessary, forbidden or not necessary?** (a) necessary (b) necessary (c) forbidden (d) not necessary (e) necessary.
**Step 2: If it is necessary, who makes the rule?** (a) the doctor (outside) → **have to**. (b) I decide myself → **must**.
**Step 3: Forbidden → mustn't.** (c) You **mustn't** touch that wire!
**Step 4: Not necessary → don't have to.** (d) We **don't have to** get up early.
**Step 5: Past time → had to.** (e) *Last year* → my brother **had to** work on Saturdays.
**Tip:** In (a) *must* is not wrong, but *have to* is better because the rule comes from the doctor.

cards.answer: (a) have to (b) must (c) mustn't (d) don't have to (e) had to

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A notice at the zoo: "Visitors ____ feed the animals." (Feeding is not allowed.)
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Feeding is **not allowed**, so it is forbidden.

**Step 2:** Forbidden = **mustn't**.

**Step 3:** *don't have to* would mean *you can choose* – wrong here. *must* means it is necessary.

**Tip:** mustn't = STOP, don't do it. don't have to = you are free to choose.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: My new school is near my house, so I ____ take a bus any more. I can walk.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "I can walk" shows the bus is **not necessary**.

**Step 2:** Not necessary = **don't have to**.

**Step 3:** *mustn't* would mean taking the bus is forbidden – that is not the meaning.

**Tip:** If you can choose, use don't have to.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: When my father was a student, he ____ walk ten kilometres to school every day.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "When my father was a student" is **past** time.

**Step 2:** *must* has no past form, so we use **had to**.

**Step 3:** *musted* is not a word; *has to* is present.

**Tip:** Past obligation = had to (for every person: I/you/he/they had to).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I ____ remember to call Aster tonight. It's her birthday and I don't want to forget.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** It is necessary, and the speaker decides it himself ("I don't want to forget").

**Step 2:** A personal feeling of necessity = **must**.

**Step 3:** *mustn't* = forbidden, *don't have to* = not necessary, *had to* = past. None fit.

**Tip:** must = I feel it is necessary; have to = someone else made the rule.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "You ____ come with us if you don't want to." Choose the best modal.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "if you don't want to" shows a free choice.

**Step 2:** No obligation is expressed by don't have to.

**Step 3:** "mustn't" would forbid coming, which does not fit.

**Tip:** Ask: is it necessary (must / have to), not allowed (mustn't), not necessary (don't have to) or a good idea (should)? For a guess: must = sure yes, can't = sure no, might = maybe.

cards.title: Step by step: should have (regret)
cards.problem: Complete: "I failed the biology exam. I ____ (study) harder instead of wasting my time on my phone."

steps.text: **Step 1: What happened?** I did **not** study hard, and now I am sorry.
**Step 2: Choose the modal.** A past regret (a good idea, but I didn't do it) → **should have** + 3rd form.
**Step 3: Compare.** *must have studied* means "I am sure I studied" – the wrong meaning here.

cards.title: Step by step: mustn't or don't have to?
cards.problem: Complete: "Lab rule: you ____ enter the chemistry room without safety goggles."

steps.text: **Step 1: What does the rule say?** Entering without goggles is **not allowed**.
**Step 2: Choose.** not allowed → **must not (mustn't)**.
**Step 3: Compare.** *don't have to* = it is not necessary – the wrong meaning for a safety rule.

cards.title: Modals for inference
rule: Use these words when you **guess** something from a **clue** you can see or know.
Almost sure it is **true** → **must be**: *Saba has worked in the field all day. She **must be** tired.*
Almost sure it is **not true** → **can't be**: *That **can't be** Lula; she is in Keren today.*
About the **past**, add **have + 3rd form** (gone, eaten, rained): *The road is wet. It **must have rained** in the night.* *He **can't have seen** us; he was asleep.*

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She must has left."

steps.text: **Step 1: Remember the rule.** After *must* the next verb is always plain: *must be, must go, must have*.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** *must **has*** ✗ – *has* has an -s, and modals never take -s after them.
**Step 3: Correct it.** *She must **have left**.* (= I am sure she left.)

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: *It isn't necessary to translate every word.*

options.A: You don't have to translate every word.
options.B: You must not translate any word.
options.C: You have to translate almost all of the words.
options.D: You must translate all of the words.
options.E: It isn't necessary to translate any word.

cards.why:
The phrase 'It isn't necessary' expresses a **lack of obligation**. In English, the modal phrase **'don't have to'** is used to show that something is not required or necessary. 

*   **'Must not'** (Option B) means prohibition (you are forbidden).
*   **'Have to'** (Option C/D) means obligation (you are required).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Her eyes are red and she is holding a tissue. She ____ have been crying.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The evidence (red eyes, tissue) makes the speaker nearly sure.

**Step 2:** must have + past participle = strong inference about the past.

**Step 3:** "can't have" would mean she surely was not crying.

**Tip:** Ask: is it necessary (must / have to), not allowed (mustn't), not necessary (don't have to) or a good idea (should)? For a guess: must = sure yes, can't = sure no, might = maybe.

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The speaker thinks it is possible because of the usual time.

**Step 2:** could/might/may express possibility.

**Step 3:** "can't" means impossible; "mustn't" is prohibition.

**Tip:** Ask: is it necessary (must / have to), not allowed (mustn't), not necessary (don't have to) or a good idea (should)? For a guess: must = sure yes, can't = sure no, might = maybe.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Aster has been studying and living in London for ten years, so she ________ speak English very fluently.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Ten years in London is strong evidence – we are sure about now.

**Step 2:** Sure about the present → **must** + plain verb (*must speak*).

**Step 3:** *must have* is for the past and needs a 3rd form (*must have spoken*).

**Tip:** must / have to = necessary; mustn't = not allowed; don't have to = not necessary; should = a good idea. Guessing: must = sure yes, can't = sure no, might = maybe. Add have + 3rd form for the past.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The soccer field is completely covered in puddles; it ________ heavily during the night.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** We see puddles now, so we are sure it rained in the night.

**Step 2:** Sure about the past → **must have** + 3rd form → **must have rained**.

**Step 3:** *should have rained* would mean it was a good idea for it to rain – that makes no sense.

**Tip:** must / have to = necessary; mustn't = not allowed; don't have to = not necessary; should = a good idea. Guessing: must = sure yes, can't = sure no, might = maybe. Add have + 3rd form for the past.

glossary.meaning: A small helping verb (must, should, can, might) before a main verb. It adds a meaning like "necessary" or "possible". The verb after it is plain: no to, no -s.

cards.title: Gerunds, infinitives and participles
rule: **Step 1 – after some verbs use -ing:** *enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, can't help*: *I enjoy **climbing** Emba Soira.*
**Step 2 – after other verbs use to + verb:** *want, decide, hope, plan, agree, attempt*: *We decided **to camp** near Filfil.*
**Step 3 – after a small word like in, at, of, about, without, use -ing:** *She is good **at drawing**.*
**to + verb** can also tell **why** (purpose): *She went to the market **to buy** berbere.*
**-ing or -ed?** The thing that **causes** the feeling takes **-ing**: *an **amazing** trip*. The person who **has** the feeling takes **-ed**: *We were **amazed***.

cards.title: Step by step: -ing or to + verb?
cards.problem: Complete: (a) We enjoy ____ (walk) along the beach in Massawa. (b) They decided ____ (travel) to Nakfa by bus. (c) She is interested in ____ (learn) Arabic. (d) He went to the market ____ (buy) coffee beans. (e) The football match was ____ (excite); we were all ____ (excite).

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the word just before the gap.**
**Step 2: enjoy / avoid / finish → -ing.** (a) enjoy **walking**.
**Step 3: want / decide / hope / plan → to + verb.** (b) decided **to travel**.
**Step 4: a small word like in / at / of / about → -ing.** (c) interested in **learning**.
**Step 5: Why did he go? → to + verb (purpose).** (d) **to buy**.
**Step 6: cause → -ing, feeling → -ed.** (e) The match was **exciting**; we were **excited**.

cards.title: Step by step: Future continuous
body: **Step 1:** Form: will + be + verb-ing: "I will be studying." Negative: won't be + -ing. Question: Will you be + -ing?
**Step 2:** Use 1: an action that will be going on at a time in the future: "At 8 pm tomorrow I will be watching the match."
**Step 3:** Use 2: a longer action that will be going on when something short happens: "When you arrive, we will be having dinner."
**Step 4:** Use 3: polite questions about someone's plans: "Will you be using the computer this evening?"
**Step 5:** Time words: this time tomorrow, at 6 o'clock next Monday, this time next week. Do not use it with state verbs (know, like, own).

cards.title: Noun clauses
rule: A **noun clause** is a small sentence (with its own subject and verb) inside a bigger sentence. It does the job of a noun. It starts with **that, what, whether / if, who, where, when, why, how**.

It can stand in **three places**: before the main verb (**subject**): ***What you told me** was true.* After the verb (**object**): *I know **that he is honest**.* After *is / was* (**complement**): *The problem is **that we have no time**.*
Inside it, use **statement order** (subject + verb), not question order: *I don’t know **where she lives*** (not *where does she live*).
If the main verb is past (*said, asked, thought*), the verb in the noun clause usually moves into the past too: *He said **that he was** ready.*
A noun clause before the main verb counts as **one thing** → singular verb: ***What we need is** more books.*

rule: A noun clause can be the **subject** of a sentence. It comes **before the main verb**, just like a noun: ***What you told me** was true.* (compare: ***The story** was true.*)

**How to find it:** find the main verb (*was, is, surprised, depends*…). Everything before it is the subject. If you can replace it with *It* or *This*, it is a noun-clause subject: ***That he passed** surprised everyone.* → *It surprised everyone.*
A noun-clause subject is **singular**: *What we need **is** more books.* *Why they left **is** a mystery.*
Starters: **That** (a fact), **What / Whatever** (a thing), **Whether** (yes/no – at the start use *whether*, not *if*), **Who / Whoever, Where, When, Why, How**.
Inside the clause use **statement order** (subject + verb): ***Where she lives** is a secret* (not *Where does she live*).
A long subject can move to the end with **It**: *That he lied is clear.* = ***It** is clear **that he lied**.*

cards.problem: Join the sentences. Start with a noun clause. (a) He passed the exam. It surprised everyone. (b) Where did they hide the money? It is still a secret. (c) Will the school open on Monday? It depends on the rain.

steps.text: **Step 1: Choose the starter.** (a) a fact → *That*. (b) a wh-question → keep *Where*. (c) a yes/no question → *Whether*.
**Step 2: Change question order to statement order.** *did they hide* → *they hid*; *Will the school open* → *the school will open*.
**Step 3: Put the clause before the verb and drop *It*.**
(a) **That he passed the exam** surprised everyone.
(b) **Where they hid the money** is still a secret.
(c) **Whether the school will open on Monday** depends on the rain.
**Check:** the verb after the clause is singular: *surprised, is, depends*.

cards.title: SVC sentences and adjectival complements
rule: **SVC = Subject + linking Verb + Complement.** A **linking verb** (*be, become, seem, look, feel, get*) does not show an action. It joins the subject to a word that describes it.
After a linking verb use an **adjective** (or a noun), **not an -ly word**: *The problem **seems serious*** (not *seriously*). *Many graduates **became doctors**.* *The injera **smells good**.*
An adjective can have words after it that finish its meaning (an **adjectival complement**): *I am **happy to help**.* *She is **sure that she will return**.*

**Step 1:** "are" is a linking verb.

**Step 2:** "happy" describes the subject "The children".

cards.problem:
Which sentence has the correct English word order?
A. The security guard the main gate at midnight locked.
B. The security guard locked the main gate at midnight.
C. At midnight the main gate the security guard locked.

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the three parts.** Who? *The security guard*. Does what? *locked*. What? *the main gate*.
**Step 2: Put them in English order.** who + does + what: *The security guard locked the main gate*. The time (*at midnight*) goes at the end.

Which sentence is missing a verb?

B. My brother a hard-working farmer in the village.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look for the verb.** A has *is*, C has *are*. B has no verb at all.
**Step 2: The rule.** Every English sentence needs a verb. To say what someone **is**, use *am / is / are* (past: *was / were*). This linking verb joins *my brother* to *a hard-working farmer*.
**Step 3: Watch out.** In Tigrinya *እዩ* comes at the end (ሓወይ ኣብቲ ዓዲ ትጉህ ሓረስታይ እዩ). Do not drop it in English.

cards.title: Adjective (relative) clauses
rule: An **adjective clause** is a group of words that **describes a noun**. It comes right after the noun and starts with **who** (people), **which** (things), **that** (people or things), **whose** (belonging to), **where** (places) or **when** (times): *The doctor **who works in Keren** is my aunt.*

**No commas** = the clause tells us **which one**: *Students **who study abroad** often stay there.* **With commas** = the clause only adds **extra** information; we already know who it is: *Asmara, **which is the capital**, is very clean.* Never use *that* after a comma.
Do not repeat the noun with *he / she / it*: ✗ *My brother who lives in Assab **he** is a nurse.* ✔ *My brother who lives in Assab is a nurse.*

units.intro: Grammar: will, should and might for how sure we are, and groups of words that tell when, why, how or for what purpose (so that, in order to, lest, although).

lessons.title: Modals of inference: will, should, might

cards.title: Modals of inference: will, should, might
rule: These words show **how sure** you are about something. **will** = very sure (about 100%): *Prices **will be** higher next year.*
**should** = I expect it (about 80%): *The bus left Asmara at 7, so it **should be** in Keren by 9.*
**might / may** = maybe (about 50%): *We **might** need more money for the wedding.*
Negative: **won't** = sure it will not happen; **might not** = maybe not. After will / should / might use the plain verb (no *to*): *It might rain* (not *might to rain*).

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The speaker says "I'm not sure".

**Step 2:** might expresses possibility.

**Step 3:** must and will are too certain; can't means impossible.

**Tip:** How sure? will (very sure) → should (expected) → might (maybe). Purpose: to / in order to + verb; so that + subject + verb. lest = so that … not. although + subject + verb; despite + noun or -ing.

cards.title: Step by step: will, should or might?
cards.problem: Complete: (a) Don't worry about the fees – my father ____ pay them; he has already got the money. (b) The bus left Asmara at 7, so it ____ be in Keren by 9. (c) I'm not sure, but prices ____ go down after the harvest.

steps.text: **Step 1: How sure is the speaker?** Look for clue words.
**Step 2: very sure → will.** (a) *he has already got the money* → **will**.
**Step 3: expected (it normally happens) → should.** (b) a normal journey time → **should**.
**Step 4: maybe → might.** (c) *I'm not sure* → **might**.

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Studying every day makes passing **expected**.

**Step 2:** expected → **should**.

**Step 3:** *can't* and *might not* say the opposite; *mustn't* means not allowed.

**Tip:** How sure? will (very sure) → should (expected) → might (maybe). Purpose: to / in order to + verb; so that + subject + verb. lest = so that … not. although + subject + verb; despite + noun or -ing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Take an umbrella. It ____ rain this afternoon – the sky is grey, but I'm not sure.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *I'm not sure* = maybe.

**Step 2:** maybe → **might**.

**Step 3:** *will certainly* and *must* are too sure; *can't* = sure it won't.

**Tip:** How sure? will (very sure) → should (expected) → might (maybe). Purpose: to / in order to + verb; so that + subject + verb. lest = so that … not. although + subject + verb; despite + noun or -ing.

cards.title: Adverbial phrases and clauses
rule: An **adverbial** answers *when? where? why? how?* or *for what purpose?* A **phrase** has no subject + verb (*in the morning, to save money, despite the rain*). A **clause** has a subject + verb (*because prices rose, so that we can save, although she earns a lot*).
**Purpose (why you do it):** *to / in order to* + verb; *so that* + subject + can / will: *I walk to school **so that** I can save money.*

**To stop something bad happening:** *so as not to* + verb, or *lest* + subject + (should) + verb (*lest* is formal and means "so that … not"): *Write your expenses down **lest** you **forget** them.*
**Contrast (a surprise):** *although / even though* + subject + verb; *despite / in spite of* + a noun or -ing. Use only **one** linker: ✗ *Although…, but…*

units.title: Following Instructions
units.intro: Grammar: how word endings show the word type (noun, adjective, verb, adverb), and polite indirect questions (Could you tell me where the bank is?).

cards.title: Parts of speech from affixes
rule: The **ending** of a word often tells you its type. **Nouns** (things, ideas): -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -er/-or (*instruction, payment, kindness, ability, baker*). **Adjectives** (describe a noun): -ful, -less, -ous, -able, -ive, -al (*useful, careless, famous, reliable, active, national*).
**Verbs** (actions): -ise/-ize, -en, -ify (*organise, shorten, clarify*). **Adverbs** (how something is done): -ly (*carefully*).
Some endings do **not** change the word type; they only change its form: -s (*books, runs*), -ed (*played*), -ing (*playing*), -er/-est (*taller, tallest*).
**How to choose:** look at the word before the gap. After *the / a* → noun. After *very / is* → adjective. After *to / will / can* → verb. After an action → adverb: *Mix the flour **carefully**.*

**Step 1:** The suffix -ly often makes adverbs from adjectives.

**Step 2:** "carefully" describes how an action is done.

**Step 3:** The others are an adjective and nouns.

**Tip:** Word endings: -tion / -ment / -ness = noun; -ful / -less / -ous / -able = adjective; -ify / -ise / -en = verb; -ly = adverb. Indirect question = polite start + subject + verb, no do/does/did; yes/no → if / whether.

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the plural nouns.** A: *crisises*. B: *children*. C: *analyses*.
**Step 2: Remember the special plural.** Words ending in **-is** change to **-es**: *crisis → crises, analysis → analyses, thesis → theses*.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the word before the gap.**
**Step 2: after *the* → a noun.** (a) **instructions** (-tion).
**Step 3: after *very* / *is* → an adjective.** (b) **useful** (-ful).
**Step 4: after an action (*mix*) → an adverb.** (c) **slowly** (-ly).
**Step 5: after *can / to / will* → a verb.** (d) **clarify** (-ify).

**Tip:** Word endings: -tion / -ment / -ness = noun; -ful / -less / -ous / -able = adjective; -ify / -ise / -en = verb; -ly = adverb. Indirect question = polite start + subject + verb, no do/does/did; yes/no → if / whether.

cards.title: Direct and indirect questions
rule: A **direct question**: *Where is the station?* An **indirect question** is more polite: *Could you tell me **where the station is**?*
**Step 1:** Start politely: *Could you tell me… / Do you know… / I wonder…*
**Step 2:** Use **statement order**: subject + verb (*the station is*).
**Step 3:** Take out **do / does / did** and put the tense on the main verb: *What time does the bus leave?* → *Do you know what time the bus **leaves**?*
**Step 4:** A yes/no question uses **if** or **whether**: *Is the shop open?* → *Do you know **if** the shop is open?*

cards.title: Step by step: a past question with "did"
cards.problem: Complete: The teacher asked Dawit, "Why ____ (not / complete) your assignment yesterday?"

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the tense.** *yesterday* → past simple.
**Step 2: Make the question.** question word + **didn't** + subject + **plain verb**.
**Step 3: Check the verb.** *did* already shows the past, so the verb stays plain: *complete* (✗ *completed*).

cards.title: Step by step: reporting a yes/no question
cards.problem: The director asked me, "Will you come to the meeting tomorrow?" Report it: The director asked me ________ to the meeting the next day.

steps.text: **Step 1: What kind of question?** It can be answered yes or no → use **whether** (or **if**).
**Step 2: Statement order.** subject + verb: *I would come* (not *would I come*).
**Step 3: Move the tense back.** *asked* is past, so *will* → **would**; *you* → *I*; *tomorrow* → *the next day*.

cards.title: Step by step: reporting a "Don't…" command
cards.problem: The principal said to the students, "Don't run inside the laboratory." Report it: The principal warned the students ________ inside the laboratory.

steps.text: **Step 1: What kind of sentence?** A command that starts with *Don't*.
**Step 2: The pattern.** told / warned / asked + person + **not to** + plain verb.
**Step 3: Put *not* first.** *warned the students **not to run***.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She told me that she ________ her university application the day before.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** She said: "I submitted my application **yesterday**." In the report, *yesterday* becomes *the day before*.

**Step 2:** After *told* (past), the past simple moves one step back → had + 3rd form → **had submitted**.

**Step 3:** *submitted* does not show that it happened before she spoke; *has submitted* is not used after a past reporting verb here.

**Tip:** Reported question: asked + if/whether (or a wh-word) + subject + verb. Move the tense one step back: past → had + 3rd form, will → would.

**In Tigrinya:** 'The day before' (እቲ ቅድሚኡ ዝነበረ መዓልቲ) ዝብል ሓረግ እቲ ዋና ዘረባ ኣብ past simple (yesterday) ከም ዝነበረ ይሕብረና። ስለዚ ምስቲ 'told' ዝብል ሕሉፍ ግሲ ተሓዊሱ ናብ Past Perfect ክሰግም ስለ ዘለዎ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'had submitted' (Option C) እዩ።

**Step 1:** The officer asked: "Where **did** you park your car?"

units.intro: Grammar: making the verb match the real subject in long sentences, and the passive with has/have been and had been (has been built, had been stolen).

cards.title: Agreement in complex sentences
rule: In long sentences other words can stand between the subject and the verb. **Step 1:** find the real subject (the main noun). **Step 2:** cover the words between it and the verb. **Step 3:** make the verb match: *The **rights** of every citizen **are** protected.* *The **list** of complaints **is** long.*
In a *who / which / that* part, the verb matches the noun just before *who / which / that*: *people who **are** …; a person who **is** …*
The title of one book or film is **one** thing → singular: *“Things Fall Apart” **is** a famous novel.*

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The houses that my uncle built ____ very strong.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The main subject is "The houses" (plural).

**Step 2:** "that my uncle built" is a relative clause and does not change agreement.

**Step 3:** So the verb is "are".

**Tip:** Cover the words between the subject and the verb, then match the verb to the real subject. Passive: has/have been + 3rd form (up to now), had been + 3rd form (before a past time).

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
**Step 1:** *police* means the police officers – it is always plural in English.

**Step 2:** Plural subject → plural verb: **are** investigating.

**Step 3:** Do not be tricked: *police* has no -s, but it is still plural.

**Tip:** Find the real subject, cover the words between it and the verb, then make the verb match the real subject.

**In Tigrinya:** 'Police' (ፖሊስ) ዝብል ስም ክትርእዮ ከለኻ ናይ ነጸላ (singular) ይመስል እምበር፡ ብሰዋስው ግን ወትሩ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ (plural) ተገይሩ ስለ ዝውሰድ ድሕሪኡ ዝመጽእ ግሲ 'are' (Option B) ክኸውን ኣለዎ።

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the real subject.** *the number* (of visitors) – one number → singular.
**Step 2: Choose the tense.** *Since…* means from then until now → present perfect.
**Step 3: Put it together.** singular + present perfect → **has increased** (not *have*).
**Remember:** *the number of* + singular verb; *a number of* (= many) + plural verb.

lessons.title: Present perfect and past perfect passive

cards.title: Present perfect and past perfect passive
rule: **Passive** = the subject does not do the action; something is done **to** it.
**has / have been + 3rd form** – from the past up to now: *New laws **have been passed** to stop discrimination.*
**had been + 3rd form** – done **before** another past time: *Before 1991 many people **had been denied** their rights.*
Do not forget **been**, and use the 3rd form (*changed, given, written*), not the plain verb.

examples.text: Women have been given equal rights.
The rule had been change.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "The rule had been change."

steps.text: **Step 1: Remember the form.** had + **been** + 3rd form.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** *change* is the plain verb. The 3rd form is *changed*.
**Step 3: Correct it.** *The rule had been **changed**.*

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **Cross out** the words between the subject and verb, then check agreement.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Find the real subject before you choose the verb: one of, the number of and titles are singular; a number of (= many) is plural. Passive: has / have been + 3rd form (up to now); had been + 3rd form (before a past time).

cards.title: Step by step: Present perfect and past perfect passive
body: **Step 1:** Present perfect passive = has/have + been + V3: "The work has been finished."
**Step 2:** Past perfect passive = had + been + V3: "The work had been finished before the manager came."
**Step 3:** To change active to passive: the object becomes the new subject, keep has/have/had, add "been" and the 3rd form.
**Step 4:** Use has with a singular subject and have with a plural subject; "had" is used for all subjects.
**Step 5:** Add "by + the doer" only when it is important who did it.

**Example:** Active: "They have repaired the road." → Passive: "The road has been repaired." Active: "Somebody had stolen the money before the police arrived." → "The money had been stolen before the police arrived."

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Perfect passive = HAVE + BEEN + V3" (H-B-3); past perfect just turns HAVE into HAD.
body: "Perfect passive = HAVE + BEEN + V3" (H-B-3); past perfect just turns HAVE into HAD.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Do not forget "been": "The road has repaired" is wrong because roads cannot repair. Check that the new subject cannot do the action itself.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The number of students _______ greater this year than that of last year.
cards.why:
There is a specific rule for 'The number of' vs 'A number of':
1. **'The number of'** takes a **singular verb** (referring to the specific total).
2. **'A number of'** takes a **plural verb** (meaning 'many').
Since it refers to 'this year', the singular present verb **'is'** is correct.

cards.q: The rare African manuscript ________ from the national archives before the guards noticed the broken window.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Two past actions: first the manuscript was stolen, then the guards noticed.

**Step 2:** The earlier action takes had + 3rd form; the manuscript did not steal → passive.

**Step 3:** had been + 3rd form → **had been stolen**.

**Tip:** If the subject does not do the action, use the passive: the right form of be + 3rd form (was given, is being raised, will have been printed).

cards.title: Step by step: past simple passive
cards.problem: Complete: "The official report ____ (submit) by the committee before the deadline last night."

steps.text: **Step 1: Who does the action?** The committee submits the report. The report does not submit anything → **passive**.
**Step 2: Find the tense.** *last night* → past simple.
**Step 3: Make the passive.** was/were + 3rd form → singular *report* → **was submitted**.

cards.title: Step by step: present continuous passive
cards.problem: Complete: "A lot of money ____ currently ____ (raise) to build the new school library."

steps.text: **Step 1: Who does the action?** People raise the money; the money does not raise anything → **passive**.
**Step 2: Find the tense.** *currently* = now → present continuous.
**Step 3: Make the passive.** is/are + **being** + 3rd form → *money* is singular → **is being raised**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The high school teacher ________ a beautiful traditional gift by the students on her graduation day.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The teacher did not give the gift – she **received** it from the students (*by the students*).

**Step 2:** So we need the passive: was + 3rd form → **was given**.

**Step 3:** *gave* would mean that the teacher gave the gift.

**Tip:** If the subject does not do the action, use the passive: the right form of be + 3rd form (was given, is being raised, will have been printed).

**In Tigrinya:** እቲ መምህር ባዕሉ ህያብ ኣይሃበን፤ ኣብ ክንዲኡ ካብ ተመሃሮ ህያብ ተዋሂብዎ (received)። እዚ ዓይነት መዋቕር ድርብ ተቐባሊ ዘለዎ ግሲ ኮይኑ፡ 'was given' (Option B - ተዋሂቡ) ቅኑዕ መልሲ ይኸውን። 'gave' እንተይልና እቲ መምህር ባዕሉ ንተመሃሮ ህያብ ሂብዎም ማለት ምኾነ።

**Step 1:** Papers cannot print themselves → **passive**.

units.title: Fashion
units.intro: Grammar: am/is/are + -ing for actions going on around now, confusing word pairs (accept/except, adapt/adopt), and have/has been + -ing (present perfect continuous) for actions from the past up to now.

lessons.title: Present continuous for a period of time

cards.title: Present continuous for a period of time
rule: **am / is / are + -ing** is for actions happening **now**, and also for actions going on **around now**, over a period: *this week, this month, this year, these days*: *My bicycle is broken, so I **am walking** to school this week.*
It also shows a **change that is happening**: *Fashion **is becoming** more expensive in Asmara.*
Textbook example (Lesson 8.13): *Currently, I’**m attending** a three-month programme in secretarial science.* The writer is not in class now; the course goes on for three months.
**State verbs** (*know, like, want, belong, understand*) describe a state, not an action → no -ing: *I **like** this dress* (not *am liking*).

examples.text: These days many students are learning to sew.
I am knowing this designer.
This month my aunt is staying with us in Dekemhare.

cards.title: Step by step: Confusing verbs
body: **Step 1:** lie – lay – lain (no object after it: rest flat): "I lie down after lunch." lay – laid – laid (needs an object: put something down): "She laid the book on the table."
**Step 2:** rise – rose – risen (no object: go up): "The sun rises." raise – raised – raised (needs an object: lift): "Raise your hand."
**Step 3:** sit – sat – sat (no object) vs set – set – set (put something somewhere).
**Step 4:** say vs tell: say something (to someone); tell someone something: "He said that…", "He told me that…".
**Step 5:** borrow (take from someone) vs lend (give to someone); bring (towards the speaker) vs take (away from the speaker).
**Example:** "Yesterday the price of sugar (raised/rose)." → rose (no object). "Can you (borrow/lend) me your pen?" → lend. "She (said/told) me the answer." → told (a person follows).

cards.title: Present perfect continuous: form and use
rule: **Form:** have/has + been + verb-ing. *I **have been waiting**. She **has been studying**.*
**Negative:** have/has + not + been + -ing: *They **haven't been sleeping** well.* **Question:** Have/Has + subject + been + -ing? ***Has** she **been working** here long?*
**Use 1 – it started in the past and is still going on now** (often with *for, since, How long…?*): *I **have been learning** English **for** six years.* *It **has been raining since** 8 o'clock.*
**Use 2 – it has just stopped and we can see the result now:** *Your eyes are red. **Have** you **been crying**?* *I'm hot because I**'ve been running**.*
**Use 3 – it happened again and again recently, up to now** (*recently, lately, these days*): *I**'ve been getting up** early **lately**.*
**for** + a period of time (*for two hours, for a week*); **since** + the starting point (*since Monday, since 2020, since I was ten*).
State verbs (*know, like, believe, own, understand*) do not take -ing: *I **have known** her for years* (not *have been knowing*).
**Not the past continuous:** *was/were + -ing* is for a moment in the **past** (*At 8 last night I **was reading***). *have been + -ing* reaches **now** (*I **have been reading** since 8*).

body: In Lesson 8.13 the writer of the job letter says: *Currently, I**'m attending** a three-month programme in secretarial science.* That is the **present continuous**: an action that goes on over a period around now.

cards.q: We ____ for the bus for forty minutes, and it still hasn't come.

**Step 1:** *for forty minutes* + *it still hasn't come* → the waiting started in the past and is still going on.

**Step 2:** Use **have been + -ing**: *have been waiting*.

**Step 3:** *are waiting* does not show how long; *had waited* is past perfect.

**Tip:** for/since + still going on → present perfect continuous.

cards.title: Quick check

**Step 1:** *since she finished university* gives the starting point; she still works there.

**Step 2:** Started in the past + still true now → **has been working**.

**Step 3:** *is working* is a common mistake: English does not use the present continuous with *since*.

**Tip:** since + a starting point → have/has (been).

cards.title: Quick check

**Step 1:** We can see a result now (dirty hands) of an activity that has just stopped.

**Step 2:** Use the present perfect continuous: *What have you been doing?*

**Step 3:** *have you done* asks about a finished result, not the activity that made your hands dirty.

**Step 2:** Result / how many → present perfect: **have read**.

**Step 3:** *have been read* is a passive form – wrong here.

**Tip:** How many? → have + V3. How long? → have been + -ing.

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
**Step 1:** *at 8 o'clock last night* is a moment in the past. It is finished now.

**Step 2:** An action in progress at a past moment → past continuous: **were having**.

**Step 3:** *have been having* would connect the action to **now** – but last night is not now.

**Tip:** Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day / lately → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + 3rd form. At a past moment (at 8 last night, when…) → was/were + -ing. Finished time (yesterday, ago) → past, never have been.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: I have been owning this bicycle since 2022.
options.B: I have owned this bicycle since 2022.
options.C: I am owning this bicycle since 2022.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** *own* is a state verb: it never takes -ing.

**Step 2:** From 2022 until now → present perfect simple: **have owned**.

**Step 3:** *own … since* (present simple) is wrong: *since* needs have/has.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Lately, my brother ____ to work by bus, because his car is broken.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *Lately* = again and again in the last days or weeks, up to now.

**Step 2:** A repeated activity up to now → **has been going**.

**Step 3:** *has gone* means one trip with a result (he is there now) – not a repeated activity.

**Tip:** Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day / lately → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + 3rd form. At a past moment (at 8 last night, when…) → was/were + -ing. Finished time (yesterday, ago) → past, never have been.

units.title: Making the Right Choices
units.intro: Grammar: choosing the right tense from the time words, confusing verbs, and the present simple in newspaper headlines.

cards.title: Tense review
rule: **Present simple** – habits and facts: *Water **boils** at 100 °C. My mother **makes** coffee every morning.*
**Present continuous** – happening now: *Look! The children **are dancing**.*
**Past simple** – a finished time in the past (*yesterday, ago, in 2010*): *I **saw** him yesterday.*
**Present perfect** (have/has + 3rd form) – something in the past that matters now, with *ever, never, already, yet, just, recently, since, for*: *I **have** just **finished** my exams.*
**Future perfect** (will have + 3rd form) – finished **before** a future time: *By June I **will have finished** Grade 10.*

examples.text: She has lived here since 2015.
I have seen him yesterday.
By 2030 we will have built many schools.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Examination papers are collected by an invigilator at the end of the exam. (Choose the correct active form)

options.A: Examination papers collected by the invigilator at the end of the exam.
options.B: An invigilator collected examination papers at the end of the exam.
options.C: At the end of the exam, examination papers were collected by the invigilator.
options.D: Examination papers are collected by the invigilator at the end of the exam.
options.E: An invigilator collects examination papers at the end of the exam.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The passive sentence is in the **Present Simple** ("are collected").
**Step 2:** The active form must be in the Present Simple. The agent is "an invigilator" (singular).
**Step 3:** "An invigilator collects" is the correct active form.

cards.title: Step by step: present simple with he / she / it
cards.problem: Complete: "Every morning, my father ____ (drink) a cup of coffee before he walks to his office."

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the time words.** *Every morning* = a habit → present simple.
**Step 2: Find the subject.** *my father* = he → add **-s** to the verb.
**Step 3: Answer.** *my father **drinks***.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: While we ________ for the school bus, it suddenly started to rain heavily.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *While* + a long action in the past → past continuous (was/were + -ing).

**Step 2:** The subject is *we* → **were waiting**.

**Step 3:** The short action (*it started to rain*) is in the past simple.

**Tip:** Habit or fact → present simple. Happening now → present continuous. Finished time (yesterday, ago) → past simple. Past until now (since, for, already, yet) → present perfect. Timetable → present simple. Clear sign now → going to.

**In Tigrinya:** 'While' (ክነብረና ከለና) ዝብል መስተጻምር ወትሩ ምስ ቀጻሊ ሕሉፍ እዋን (Past Continuous) እዩ ዝኸይድ። እቲ ተግባር (ምጽባይ) ነዊሕ ግዜ ዝወሰደ ኮይኑ፡ ብኻልእ ድንገታዊ ተግባር (ዝናብ ምጅማር) ተቋሪጹ። እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'we' (ብዙሕ) ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'were waiting' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Step by step: "since" → present perfect continuous
cards.problem: Complete: "Aster ____ (work) in this laboratory since she graduated from university five years ago."

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the time word.** *since she graduated* = from then until **now**.
**Step 2: Is she still working there?** Yes → the action is still going on.
**Step 3: Choose the tense.** still going on + since → present perfect continuous: **has been working** (*has worked* is also possible).
**Watch out:** ✗ *is working since…* – English does not use the present continuous with *since*.

cards.title: Step by step: "ago" → past simple

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the time word.** *three weeks ago* = a finished time in the past.
**Step 2: Choose the tense.** finished time → past simple.
**Step 3: Answer.** **completed** (✗ *has completed* – the present perfect never goes with *ago*).

cards.why:
**Step 1:** We can **see** the dark clouds now – that is a clear sign.

**Step 2:** A prediction from a sign we can see → **is going to** rain.

**Step 3:** *will* is for a decision made now or a general prediction.

**Tip:** Habit or fact → present simple. Happening now → present continuous. Finished time (yesterday, ago) → past simple. Past until now (since, for, already, yet) → present perfect. Timetable → present simple. Clear sign now → going to.

**In Tigrinya:** ኣብቲ ከባቢ ንጹር ዝኾነ ናይ ዓይኒ መርትዖ (thick dark clouds - ጸሊም ደበና) ስለ ዘሎ፡ ንመጻኢ ትንቢት ክንገልጽ ከለና 'be going to' (Option B) ክንጥቀም ኣለና። መርትዖ ምስ ዘይህሉ ግን 'will' ምጥቃም ቅኑዕ ምኾነ።

cards.why:
**Step 1:** A train leaving at a fixed time is a **timetable**.

**Step 2:** Timetables use the present simple even for the future → **departs**.

**Step 3:** Do not choose *will depart* just because you see *tomorrow*.

**Tip:** Habit or fact → present simple. Happening now → present continuous. Finished time (yesterday, ago) → past simple. Past until now (since, for, already, yet) → present perfect. Timetable → present simple. Clear sign now → going to.

**In Tigrinya:** ናይ ባቡር ወይ ነፋሪት መገሻ (timetable) ቀዋሚ ስርዓት ዘለዎ ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ንመጻኢ ግዜ ክንገልጽ ከለና ብ Present Simple 'departs' (Option B) ጥራይ ኢና ክንጽሕፍ ዘለና። 'tomorrow' ስለ ዘሎ 'will depart' ምምራጽ ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Headlines in the present simple
rule: Newspaper headlines are short. They leave out small words (*a, the, is, are*).
The **present simple** in a headline means a recent past event: ***Students Win** National Prize* = Students have won a national prize.
**to + verb** means the future: ***Minister To Open** New School* = The minister is going to open a new school.
A **3rd form alone** means a passive: ***Bridge Opened** In Keren* = A bridge has been opened in Keren.

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the parts.** Subject: LOCAL GIRL; verb: WINS; object: NATIONAL ESSAY PRIZE.
**Step 2: Restore the time.** Headlines use the present simple for a recent past event, so "wins" means "has won" (or "won").
**Step 3: Restore the missing words.** Add the articles headlines leave out: "A local girl ... the national essay prize".
**Step 4: Write the sentence.** A local girl has won the national essay prize.
**Check:** "to + verb" in a headline would mean future (GIRL TO RECEIVE PRIZE = a girl is going to receive a prize).

**Step 2:** So "TO OPEN" means "is going to open".

**Step 3:** The article "A" is omitted, as is usual in headlines.

units.intro: Grammar: comparing things with as … as, the same as, different from, -er / more … than and the -est / the most.

cards.title: Making comparisons
rule: **as + adjective + as** = equal: *Peace is **as important as** food.* **not as/so ... as** = less: *War is **not as** cheap **as** people think.*
**the same as** / **similar to** = no difference; **different from** = not the same: *My view is **different from** yours.*
**Comparatives:** short adjectives + -er (*calmer*), long adjectives more + adj (*more peaceful*), + **than**. **Superlatives:** the + -est / the most.

cards.q: Where __________ the car?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** In a simple past question, we use the auxiliary verb **did**.
**Step 2:** After **did**, the main verb must return to its **base form**. "did you park" is correct. "did you parked" is incorrect because 'parked' is already in past tense.

cards.title: Step by step: few or little?
cards.problem: Complete: "The manager said no to the plan because ____ details were given." (too few / too little / a little / much)

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the noun.** *details* ends in -s: it is a plural noun we can count.
**Step 2: Choose the word.** Countable → *few*. Uncountable → *little / much*.
**Step 3: Check the meaning.** The manager said no, so the meaning is "not enough": **too few**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Although the construction project has been delayed, ________ progress has been made this week.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *progress* is uncountable (no plural, no *a*).

**Step 2:** *a few, many, few* are only for nouns we can count.

**Step 3:** *some* works with both kinds → **some progress**.

**Tip:** Can you count it? many / few / a few + plural. Can't count it? much / little / a little. some works with both.

**In Tigrinya:** 'Progress' (ዕብየት/ምስጓም) ዘይቝጸር ስም (uncountable noun) እዩ። 'Many' ን 'a few' ን ንዝቝጸሩ ስማት ጥራይ ስለ ዝኾኑ ምስ 'progress' ክኸዱ ኣይኽእሉን። 'Some' ግን ምስ ክልቲኦም ስለ ዝኸይድ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option C እዩ።
